name: Copper peptide scalp serum

lead: Copper peptide scalp serums put GHK-Cu, a small copper-binding peptide found naturally in the body, on the scalp. Hair-loss communities add them to topical routines aiming for thicker hair and a denser hairline.

The idea draws on GHK-Cu's role in skin repair, supporting wound healing, collagen and blood vessel growth. Most GHK-Cu research is in cell and animal studies, with a few small, short facial-skin studies. No scalp hair-loss trials were found.

paras: It is used as a leave-on cosmetic serum on the scalp, typically added to a stack of other topical hair products. Users generally describe a routine of consistent use over months.
It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient. The source notes GHK-Cu also raises matrix metalloproteinases and advises caution. Scalp-specific safety data are not available.

angle.text: Hair-loss communities add copper peptide serums to topical stacks, aiming for thicker hair and a denser hairline. The idea draws on GHK-Cu's role in skin repair and follicle support. Research so far is in cells, animals and small facial-skin studies; no scalp hair trials were found.

lead: A copper peptide scalp serum is a topical product built around GHK-Cu (copper tripeptide-1), a complex of the tripeptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine and copper(II), applied to the scalp with the aim of a fuller, thicker-looking head of hair.[1] People use it as an add-on to other hair routines such as minoxidil, finasteride or microneedling, hoping it supports the follicle environment so that hair looks denser.[2][3]

GHK-Cu occurs naturally in human plasma, saliva and urine, and was isolated from plasma by Loren Pickart in 1973.[1] Its plasma level is reported to fall from about 200 ng/ml at age 20 to about 80 ng/ml by age 60, a decline that proponents link to ageing tissue.[4][5] A 2018 review lists increased hair growth, thicker hair and larger follicle size among reported effects, alongside stimulation of collagen, blood vessels and nerve outgrowth, and notes that GHK-Cu is used in skin and hair products.[6][5]

Most of the research on GHK-Cu comes from cell cultures, animal wound-healing models and facial-skin studies. A small number of laboratory studies have looked at copper-peptide complexes on hair follicles, including a 2007 study of a related copper tripeptide (AHK-Cu) on cultured human follicles and papilla cells.[7] Reviews of topical GHK note that published data on skin permeability and effectiveness are limited.[8][9] No clinical trial of a copper peptide scalp serum for hair loss has been published.
infobox: About 200 ng/ml at age 20, about 80 ng/ml at age 60[4]
Follicle size, thickness, blood supply, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects[6]
Sold as a cosmetic ingredient in skin and hair products[1]

paras: GHK-Cu is a naturally occurring tripeptide bound to copper. The GHK sequence also appears within the alpha-2 chain of type I collagen, and researchers have proposed that it is released when collagen is broken down after injury, acting as an early repair signal.[5] It is proposed to modulate wound healing, attract immune cells, act as an antioxidant and anti-inflammatory, and stimulate collagen and glycosaminoglycan synthesis in skin fibroblasts as well as blood vessel growth.[1]

Scalp serums apply the same ingredient, directly to the scalp. They are typically used alongside other topical hair products rather than as a stand-alone routine, and many products combine GHK-Cu with other peptides, botanical extracts or growth-factor ingredients.[1][2]

Cosmetic formulations list the ingredient under the name copper tripeptide-1.[1] Copper peptides are also sold as facial serums, eye creams and body products, and some looksmaxxing discussion of GHK-Cu concerns those skin uses rather than the scalp.[10][11]

Pickart worked on the peptide beginning with his doctoral research in the early 1970s. In the discovery experiments, liver tissue from older donors was incubated in plasma from younger donors, and the older tissue began producing proteins more typical of younger tissue, which pointed to a small plasma factor.[5] He isolated a copper-binding peptide from human plasma albumin in 1973, and in 1977 the growth-modulating factor was identified as glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine.[1]

In 1980 Pickart and colleagues proposed that GHK might help carry copper into cells.[1] During the 1980s, Maquart and colleagues reported that GHK-Cu stimulated collagen synthesis in fibroblast cultures, a finding that underlies much of the later cosmetic interest.[1]

subs.h: From wound care to hair and skin products
paras: Wound-healing studies followed: a 2003 rat study of ischemic open wounds reported a larger reduction in wound size with GHK-Cu than with vehicle or no treatment, and rabbit and diabetic-rat studies in 2006 to 2008 reported improved wound contraction and blood vessel growth.[1] Cosmetic companies adopted copper peptides for anti-ageing creams and for hair-loss prevention products.[1]

By 2003 copper peptide hair products were already being discussed on bodybuilding and hair-loss forums as an add-on to minoxidil, with one T Nation poster naming a product called Folligen and asking why wider acceptance had not followed.[2]

Reviews describe GHK as stimulating blood vessel and nerve outgrowth, increasing collagen, elastin and glycosaminoglycan synthesis, supporting dermal fibroblasts, and showing anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions.[6] The review authors also summarise gene-expression data, reporting that GHK changes the activity of a large number of human genes, and propose that this explains how one small molecule could influence many pathways.[6] Proponents extend these actions to the hair follicle, whose size and surrounding blood supply are linked to hair thickness.[5]

In the wider literature, GHK-Cu is reported to release growth factors such as VEGF and BDNF in cell models and to act on both matrix metalloproteinases and their inhibitors.[1] The Wikipedia entry notes that because it raises enzymes that break down matrix proteins, it should be used with caution, and that more research is needed.[1]

Delivery is a recurring topic. A 2025 review of topical GHK as an anti-wrinkle peptide says GHK-Cu and its palmitoylated derivative are widely used in cosmetics, but that published information on skin permeability and effectiveness is insufficient.[8] A 2025 review of liposome-encapsulated GHK-Cu says free GHK-Cu is fairly hydrophilic with limited penetration through the outer skin layer, and that liposomes may improve it.[9]

sections.h: Laboratory and animal research relevant to hair
paras: A 2007 study in Archives of Pharmacal Research examined a related copper tripeptide, AHK-Cu, on human hair follicles and dermal papilla cells. At low concentrations the compound promoted hair follicle elongation in ex vivo culture and increased dermal papilla cell proliferation, and it shifted apoptosis-related markers in a direction that reduces cell death, although the reduction in apoptotic cells was not statistically significant. The authors suggested it promotes growth by stimulating proliferation and inhibiting apoptosis.[7]

A 2020 study in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open tested injectable hair-growth formulations (QR678 and QR678 Neo) that combine growth factors and peptides, with one containing copper tripeptide-1. Cell assays found the components safe, mice showed hair growth at injection sites, and a chemotherapy-induced hair-loss model was used to test follicle viability. The authors concluded that human trials in chemotherapy-related alopecia were justified.[12]
These studies concern a different copper tripeptide, an injected multi-ingredient formulation, or laboratory models, so they do not describe the effect of a GHK-Cu serum applied to a human scalp.

No studies found on copper peptide scalp serums for hair loss. Related human work on GHK-Cu comes from skin. A randomised trial examined a copper tripeptide complex skin-care regimen after CO2 laser resurfacing.[13] The 2018 review summarises further facial studies: a 12-week facial cream study in 71 women with photoaged skin that reported greater skin density and thickness and fewer fine lines, a 12-week eye-cream study in 41 women compared with placebo and vitamin K cream, and a thigh-skin study in which collagen production improved in 70 percent of women using GHK-Cu, versus 50 percent with a vitamin C cream and 40 percent with retinoic acid.[5] An 8-week randomised, double-blind trial summarised in the same review reported a 31.6 percent reduction in wrinkle volume versus Matrixyl 3000.[5]

Reviewers describe these skin studies as small and short, and call for further research.[1][8][4] A 2026 sports-medicine review of peptide therapies, including GHK-Cu, says rigorous human safety data are scarce for many unapproved peptides.[14]

Copper peptides are sold as cosmetic ingredients, which in most jurisdictions are regulated differently from drugs: they are not approved as hair-loss drugs. Approved hair-loss treatments such as topical minoxidil and oral finasteride are separate, drug-regulated products.

Scalp-specific safety data for GHK-Cu are not available. The general GHK-Cu literature notes that it influences matrix-degrading enzymes as well as their inhibitors and advises caution.[1] Injectable GHK-Cu discussed on forums is a separate matter from cosmetic serums; sports-medicine reviewers note that injectable peptides outside approved products lack rigorous safety data.[14][15]

Copper peptide serums are discussed in hair-loss communities as an add-on to minoxidil or finasteride routines. An early T Nation thread (2003) asked whether anyone had used a copper peptide hair product, Folligen being named, to thicken fine hair gained with Rogaine and spironolactone.[2]

On looksmax.org, GHK-Cu is discussed mostly for skin. Members ask whether it can reduce fine lines or calm atopic dermatitis, compare it with Matrixyl, debate it against acne treatments, and ask how it combines with microneedling.[10][16][11][3] Other threads address the stability of reconstituted GHK-Cu and whether it can be combined with isotretinoin, reflecting a broader culture of peptide experimentation that includes injecting research peptides; those practices are outside the scope of a cosmetic scalp serum and are not described here.[17][18]

Copper peptide scalp serums are often grouped with other topical and procedural hair-density options: minoxidil, finasteride, microneedling and derma rolling, platelet-rich plasma and low-level light devices. GHK-Cu is also used on facial skin in anti-ageing and post-procedure routines.[13][5]

lore.intro: Copper peptides are discussed in hair-loss forums as an extra to established treatments, and on looksmax.org mostly as a skin product with a growing set of related peptide threads.[2][10]
